newsitem.title: USA: Clinton meets Bosnian, says troops leaving on time.
newsitem.headline: Clinton meets Bosnian, says troops leaving on time.

text.p: President Bill Clinton met Bosnian President Alija Izetbegovic on Wednesday and said U.S. troops would leave the region on schedule in June 1998.

But, speaking to reporters at the start of of the 30-minute meeting, Clinton said much work had to be done in the meantime to implement outstanding provisions of the 1995 Dayton Accords that brought Bosnia's 43-month war to an end.

Before the troops leave, Izetbegovic said, the accords, in particular civilian provisions, must be fully implemented, a separate disarmament pact must be enforced and Bosnia should be included in the Partnership for Peace programme under which former East Bloc countries cooperate with NATO.

Clinton told reporters as the meeting started: "There will be an international security presence (in Bosnia) for quite some time yet, during which time we have to work hard to do as much as we possibly can to implement the Dayton agreement."

Asked if he expected the nearly 8,000 U.S. peacekeeping troops to leave on schedule by June, 1998, Clinton replied: "I do. I think we all understood that you couldn't have an international security presence in the country forever."
But he said he has been calling for people in the region to focus on what can be done before that date to help the country get ready to stand on its own.

"There is a lot of very specific work to be done that if done and done right will make it possible for the nation to succeed and for people to be brought back into a more constructive cooperation ... when we're gone," Clinton said.
Izetbegovic said there had been major difficulties in implementing the civilian aspects of the Dayton accords and said this was a condition for withdrawal of foreign forces.
The accords, named for the Ohio town where they were negotiated by Bosnian, Serb and Croatian leaders and brokered by the United States, were signed in Paris in December, 1995.
Their key civilian elements included the establishment of a democratic government and the resettlement and free movement of minorities within the country.
"We have some problems with the process of the Dayton implementation," the Bosnian president told reporters. "... Especially the civil part is going slowly."

He cited other conditions for an eventual withdrawal, including implementing a regional arms limitation pact signed in Vienna, bringing Bosnia into the Partnership for Peace and the success of the U.S.-sponsored "equip and train" programme to help merge the Croat and Moslem armies into a single force.
"On these four conditions I believe ... foreign forces can leave Bosnia without big problems," he said.

A White House spokesman said Clinton told Izetbegovic the United States would support Bosnian participation in the Partnership for Peace but this had to be accompanied by the Moslem-Croat Bosnian Federation working and by cooperation between it and the Bosnian Serbs, which does not now exist.

On Tuesday Izetbegovich said in a speech the West should stop congratulating itself on fulfilling military aspects of the accords, which resulted in NATO-led forces in Bosnia. He warned that war could break out again if the civilian aspects were not addressed.
"If the civilian aspects of the Dayton agreement are not implemented, its military results will be null as if they never even were. We could again have war," he said.
